Let’s talk about something almost all of us fall into without realizing— outcome bias—and why focusing on the process is so important.
Picture this: a company launches a new product. They’ve done their homework—careful research, solid planning, the works. But then, the market suddenly shifts. The product flops. Instantly, everyone’s pointing fingers at the team for making a “bad” decision.
Now, flip the script. Imagine a product that gets thrown together at the last minute, with hardly any planning. But thanks to a stroke of luck, it takes off. The team gets showered with praise, even though their process was shaky at best.
See what’s happening here? We’re letting the outcome—good or bad—overshadow how the decision was actually made.
This kind of thinking is risky. It pushes people to chase lucky wins instead of making thoughtful choices. And it makes learning from experience almost impossible, because you’re judging everything by the final result, not by what you could control along the way.
So, how can you break out of this trap? It starts with focusing on how decisions are made—not just what happens after.
Ask yourself: What information was available at the time? Were different options seriously considered? Was the reasoning solid and logical? Did you reach out for different viewpoints, or just go with your gut?
When you look at each decision through that lens, you start to see patterns. You find ways to get better—regardless of whether things turned out well or not.
Here’s a simple analogy: Think of decision-making like planting seeds. A gardener can pick the perfect spot, use great soil, water just right, and still, a surprise storm or a sudden pest can ruin the crop. Should we judge the gardener by the harvest alone? Or by the care and expertise they brought to the process?
In real life, this means setting up systems that separate process from outcome. For example, teams can hold “decision audits”—where the focus is on the reasoning behind big choices, not just whether things worked out. It creates a culture where learning and improving come first.
So, what can you actually do to steer clear of outcome bias?
Review your decisions independently of the result. Seek feedback on your reasoning, not just on what happened after. Make a point of rewarding good decision-making—even when the outcome isn’t what you hoped. And always look at both successes and setbacks, asking: what was in my control, and what was just chance?
When you put process ahead of outcome, you build real resilience. You get better at adapting. And, over time, you make smarter, more confident choices—no matter what life throws your way.
